stories.headline: On Roberto Clemente Day, MLB has a Puerto Rico problem
stories.summary: The pipeline from the Hall of Famer's homeland to the major leagues is disintegrating.
stories.body:
KELVIN COLÓN WAS bouncing between ballparks in Puerto Rico last Tuesday, scouting teams in the inaugural Buzzer Beater baseball tournament, an unprecedented event featuring 32 high schools from across the island. Never had the baseball-loving nation held a full-fledged tournament featuring public schools, private schools and baseball academies.

Some teams were overmatched. The great majority of the players won't have professional baseball careers. But Colón, a scout for the Los Angeles Dodgers, was encouraged.

"There's talent here, man," Colón said. "I just left the ballpark right now, saw two guys that I could easily say are seventh-to-10th-round follows. They might end up in the 12th, 13th round, but that doesn't mean that they're not big leaguers."

Insiders from across Puerto Rico's baseball spectrum -- current and former major leaguers, front office executives, agents and scouts -- agree with Colón. Real talent exists in Puerto Rico -- and Tuesday's Roberto Clemente Day is a reminder of that. Major League Baseball's annual remembrance of the Hall of Fame outfielder, who died in a plane crash in 1972 delivering supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua, is a celebration of Clemente's marvelous career and humanitarian efforts. He's a hero across baseball-playing nations in Latin America, and nowhere more so than in his native Puerto Rico.

Clemente was the island's first baseball superstar, and his tragic death only added to his lore. He inspired generations of Puerto Ricans to pick up the sport and follow his path to the major leagues. But more than a half century after his death, nearly two dozen people interviewed for this story said that in recent years the pipeline from Puerto Rico to the majors has disintegrated.

The reasons they gave are wide-ranging, but every source pointed to one genesis for the decline: MLB's decision to include Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States, in the Rule 4 draft in 1989. The move took Puerto Ricans out of the international market, where they could sign as free agents at 16 years old, and into a player pool with high school seniors from the United States.

"We are neither one thing nor the other," an agent based in Puerto Rico said. "We're not a state, we're not independent. In the draft we're Americans, but in the Futures Game we're part of the world. They decide where to put us.

"Being part of the draft, I can tell you, is definitely what has hurt us the most."

THE DECLINE OF Puerto Rican-born major leaguers was evident this July in Philadelphia. For the first time since 1988, no Puerto Rican-born players were on either All-Star team. In the days leading up to the Midsummer Classic, just five players born in Puerto Rico were selected in the 2026 MLB draft, none of them before the 13th round. No Puerto Rican-born player has been taken in the first round since Heliot Ramos in 2017.

So far this season, 27 players born in Puerto Rico have appeared in games. In 2001, that number was 54 -- exactly twice as many. New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor, who missed more than two months with a left calf strain, leads Puerto Rican-born players with 1.9 bWAR this season. That would've ranked 13th among Puerto Rican-born players in 2001. There are also no Puerto Rican-born players on Kiley McDaniel's top 100 prospects list.

The lack of depth became apparent during the World Baseball Classic in March, when several of Puerto Rico's best active MLB players, including veterans Lindor, Carlos Correa, Jose Berrios and Javier Baez, were unable to participate, largely due to injuries. Puerto Rico's tournament ended with a quarterfinal loss to Italy.

"It's poor right now," a longtime MLB front office executive said. "You can see that from the beginning with the World Baseball Classic this year."

The issues transcend baseball. A poverty rate more than double that of Mississippi -- the poorest state in the U.S. -- leaves families unable to keep up with the showcase culture that has engulfed youth baseball in the United States. There is a lack of accessible facilities to properly train players. There are fewer competitive games for top-end talent. Other sports and entertainment options drain talent from the potential player pool.

"We are in a truly horrible place," the Puerto Rican agent said. "Like never before."

"It's f---ed," a current major leaguer said.

Carlos Delgado, who hit 473 home runs -- the most ever by a Puerto Rican -- across 17 MLB seasons, began his professional career after signing with the Toronto Blue Jays for $90,000 in October 1988. He was the penultimate Puerto Rican to sign as an international free agent before the draft was implemented on the island.

"We're victims of the draft," Delgado said in Spanish. "The draft has always hurt us."

Delgado was part of Puerto Rico's 1990s golden era, a storied group that included Hall of Famers Roberto Alomar, Edgar Martínez and Ivan Rodríguez, plus a slew of All-Stars, including Sandy Alomar Jr., Juan González, Bernie Williams, Carlos Baerga, Benito Santiago and Ruben Sierra. All were signed as international free agents before Puerto Rico was included in the draft.

MLB's decision to incorporate Puerto Rico in the draft, according to multiple people interviewed, had unforeseen negative consequences on the flow of talent to the majors. Previously, most big league franchises employed full-time scouts on the island who would invest in the development of prospects, knowing that a strong relationship -- and the right amount of money -- could convince players to sign with their organizations. With the draft, however, teams lost that control; any one of the other 29 teams could simply pick a desired player in the draft before them.

"I think the draft had a deleterious effect on Puerto Rico in terms of the developmental players," said Lou Melendez, a former MLB executive for 33 years with extensive experience in Puerto Rico. "Because clubs, in my estimation, were disincentivized from investing the way they were many years ago."

While clubs have backed off investing in Puerto Rico over the past 37 years, MLB has tried to compensate with funding and programs.

The league helped establish the Puerto Rico Baseball Academy and High School and has donated millions of dollars to it since its inception in 2001. In 2017, MLB donated $1 million to Puerto Rico for Hurricane Maria relief. In 2022, the league and the MLBPA donated $2 million for the building of a stadium for The Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy.

The league has also established Reviving Baseball in Inner Cities (RBI) programs on the island, currently runs a development program in four regions from September through May with more than 200 players, and holds a showcase every winter for the top 100 draft-eligible players, according to an MLB spokesperson.

"Puerto Rico has a long history of producing extraordinary Major League players who have made great contributions to the game both on and off the field," MLB wrote in a statement to ESPN. "We continue to invest in several programs aimed towards developing the next generation of Puerto Rican players in the big leagues."

MLB has played 49 regular-season games in Puerto Rico since 2001 and has had Puerto Rico host games in four of the six WBC tournaments, including this year's edition.

"The clubs don't invest, but the commissioner's office has," said Melendez, who served as Puerto Rico's general manager for the first three iterations of the WBC. "And it just hasn't been enough. It just hasn't been enough."

OVER THE YEARS, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela -- Latin American nations in the free agent market -- have seen major league clubs increase their investments, with more scouts and the creation of academies to help develop prospects. Theirs is far from a perfect situation; the system in the Dominican Republic is rife with corruption and exploitation. Still, 93 players from the Dominican Republic, including some of the sport's brightest stars, were on Opening Day rosters this season. Venezuela, whose pipeline has been damaged recently by political and economic instability, had 60 players on Opening Day rosters, second among countries and territories outside of the United States.

Puerto Rico, meanwhile, was left with a void in the developmental chain. Over the years, many teenage prospects have left Puerto Rico to attend high school in the U.S. That list includes Lindor, Báez and Edwin Arroyo, an infielder who was selected in the second round in 2021 and made his major league debut this season.

That's because unlike the U.S., Puerto Rico does not have an expansive high school baseball circuit. Baseball academies have been created over the past two decades in an attempt to fill the gap. The first one -- the Puerto Rico Baseball Academy and High School -- has produced multiple major leaguers, including Correa, a three-time All-Star and the only Puerto Rican ever drafted No. 1 overall. Carlos Beltrán, who became the sixth Puerto Rican inducted into the Hall of Fame in July and the first one who was drafted, opened his academy in 2011.

But the developmental gap, according to multiple sources, remains an issue. For one, neither academy offers dorm rooms for students, making accessibility an issue for many prospects. Sources also pointed to the lack of infrastructure available for high schoolers to train as a huge impediment, leaving the typical Puerto Rican draft prospect physically underdeveloped compared with his American and Latin American counterparts.

"I've always been a huge proponent of high school baseball in Puerto Rico," said Houston Astros manager Joe Espada, the only Puerto Rican manager in the majors and a second-round pick in 1996. "There are enough ballparks. And it doesn't have to be a league with 30 games. You can start with 10, 15."

The developmental deficiency continues after the draft, according to sources, making Puerto Rican prospects' rise through the minor leagues more difficult.

"You have the 18-year-old kid that signs out of an academy in Puerto Rico," a former major leaguer from Puerto Rico said. "He goes and plays ball. Where does he train during the offseason the next year? Or the year after? Or the year after? That 18-year-old kid isn't going to play in winter ball. He's not developed yet enough to play in winter ball where you have to win.

"So, where does he go? It's not like the 18-year-old kid in the United States that goes back to his unbelievable high school facility. Or goes to one of those institutions and can pay for it because there's an infrastructure in the U.S. In Puerto Rico, where do you go? A lot of them get stuck."

The quandary also extends to the classroom, according to sources. Ramos was Puerto Rico's top 2017 draft prospect when he decided to transfer from a public high school to Leadership Christian Academy, a bilingual private high school, for his senior year. The change required him to leave his family and move in with his current agent.

The San Francisco Giants drafted him 19th, and they agreed on a $3.1 million signing bonus. Looking back, the outfielder saw the move as pivotal in his preparation for draft negotiations, as he also had a commitment to Florida International University in his back pocket. On an island where most public schools lack sufficient English education, many of his peers don't have that advantage.

"There's a lot of people who don't know English in Puerto Rico," said Ramos, who was acquired by the New York Yankees last month. "So to go to the United States for college in a language you don't understand, that is intimidating."

That often hurts players' leverage when negotiating with teams, sources said, to the point that clubs believe they can select Puerto Ricans later in the draft and offer them less money than Americans knowing that their backup plans aren't as appealing.

"I've heard the comment from people that this is the island of $100K," Colón said. "Like everyone will sign for $100K or less."

Since 2018, three players from Puerto Rico have been selected in the second round and two have been taken in the third round. This year, Juriel Collazo was the island's first draft pick. He was chosen in the 13th round with the 374th selection.

SEVERAL PEOPLE INTERVIEWED for this story emphasized their belief that Puerto Rico would suffer another significant setback if MLB's recent draft proposal to the Major League Baseball Players Association were to pass. The proposal, extended in June during the parties' ongoing CBA negotiations, calls for the domestic draft to shrink from 20 rounds to 12 rounds and for players to be at least two years removed from high school graduation, rendering high school seniors ineligible.

"We never made the adjustment fully to what the draft was and what it became," the former Puerto Rican big leaguer said. "And we're looking at like 30 years ago. Culturally, we were one way for a long time. And this is the outcome. Now we're at 20 rounds and it's even more difficult."

Sources said they believe Puerto Rico would be better off returning to the international free agent market or being included in an international draft if that is introduced as part of the next collective bargaining agreement. Melendez said he supports removing Puerto Rico from the draft for five to 10 years.

"Let's run an experiment," Melendez said. "You can count the draft picks on two hands every year, so why not take them out of the draft and let's see what happens. Let's try something because what we're doing now ain't working. It's not working."

But a few warned that the change wouldn't singlehandedly repair the pipeline, which would require time and significant investment.

"We'd be competing against a huge group of people that are more developed at ages 15, 16, 17," a longtime scout in Puerto Rico said. "It would take years to figure out."

Others worry about the potential damage a change could inflict beyond baseball.

"I don't want free agency for Puerto Rico, and that has nothing to do with the game. It has to do with the social aspect," a Puerto Rican former All-Star said. "In the Dominican Republic, they're signing kids at 16 years old, but a lot of those kids leave school at 12, 13 years old to go practice every day to see if they have a chance to sign professionally.

"And what happens? The majority of the players aren't going to play in the major leagues, so what you're doing is putting a bunch of 17-, 18-year-old kids in Dominican society without a high school degree. I think if free agency were to come to Puerto Rico, maybe it wouldn't happen at first, but I think in the long term what happens in the Dominican could happen here."

Colón is now one of a dying breed: a full-time scout for an MLB club who is based in Puerto Rico. He has been with the Dodgers since 2018 after stints with the Miami Marlins and Baltimore Orioles and now splits his time between the island and South Florida -- two areas he is responsible for covering for the two-time defending World Series champions. Colón, who is also the general manager of the Caguas Criollos in the Puerto Rican winter league, said he knows of just two other full-time MLB scouts who live in Puerto Rico.

"If you're living on the island, you're doing something else to solidify that full-time role," Colón said. "I just think what's hurt Puerto Rico, it goes all the way back to the draft."

But Colón is not as pessimistic as some of his peers. He pointed to the six players from Puerto Rico, an island with a population of 3.2 million people, who made their major league debuts this season as an encouraging sign. He argued that U.S. states with similar populations don't produce those numbers, and yet "people are banging on Puerto Rico."

Some data supports his sentiment. Puerto Rico produced 25 high school draft selections in the top 20 rounds from 2021 through 2025, ranking in the top 10 each year when compared with U.S. states. Per capita, Puerto Rico produced twice as many players on Opening Day rosters this season as Venezuela, which has a population of 28.6 million, though the country's recent turmoil has significantly impacted clubs' ability to invest in and unearth talent there.

Colón sees stronger future draft classes in his scouting trips around Puerto Rico. Maybe Puerto Rico will never relive its 1990s golden era or generate a wave of All-Star talent like the one headed by Lindor, Correa and Báez in the 2010s. But he's hopeful -- to an extent.

"The forecast of the future, yeah, it's cloudy," Colón said. "I admit that part -- it's cloudy."

stories.headline: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 2
stories.summary: Will the Titans score any points against the Eagles? Can Ben Johnson solve Brian Flores' Vikings defense? Get ready for Week 2 with seven takes.
stories.body:
Who's ready to put their thinking caps on? Big-time offensive scoring was the story in Week 1 of the NFL season, but Week 2 is now right around the corner. What will it bring?

Every Tuesday of the NFL season, I'll turn the page from last week to this week with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions -- those come later in the week. They aren't concrete takeaways off the past week of NFL action, either -- those are fired off on Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain things. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games for us to really find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

This week, I'm starting off with my expectations for the schemer heavyweight fight of the century, my theories on the real skeleton key for the Bills' offense and my worry that the first shutout of the season will come this Sunday.

Here are seven things I think for Week 2.

Jump to:

Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite

Texans' offense will win games

Bengals defense is showing promise

Kincaid is the Bills' secret sauce

Titans will not score in Week 2

Lions' have an Achilles' heel on defense

Lawrence is league MVP this week

Five extra inklings

I think ... Ben Johnson is Brian Flores' kryptonite
Two heinous crimes were enacted Sunday by two of football nerddom's favorite coaches.

Let's start with Johnson. The Bears scored 59 points against the Panthers on Sunday, which is like if you scored 50 points, and then decided to score nine more points. Both running backs D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai ran for 100 yards and two touchdowns, and quarterback Caleb Williams added another two scores on scrambles of his own. And for those tracking Williams' accuracy metrics: 72.4% completion percentage with an off-target rate of only 13.8%.

Everything worked for the Bears' offense, which barely left first gear against the Panthers. The Bears will face far stiffer competition in Week 2 against the Vikings and Flores, who rendered an unbelievable performance against the Packers in Week 1.

The Vikings blitzed Jordan Love on 73.8% of his dropbacks Sunday -- the highest rate at which any quarterback has been blitzed since the 2023 season. The Packers were in a difficult position entering the game; starting left guard Aaron Banks was hurt, and the camp campaign to build up Anthony Belton at the starting right guard spot was abandoned late in the process. The Packers fielded 2024 fifth-round pick Jacob Monk at right guard and 2024 undrafted free agent Donovan Jennings at left guard. It was Jennings' first career start and Monk's second.

In an effort to insulate the young guards, the Packers kept more players in to block than basically any offense over the past few seasons. Love had three or fewer receivers in the route concept on an astonishing 15 dropbacks. Only three quarterbacks have had more such dropbacks over the past five seasons.

Flores has little interest in occupying those routes with multiple defenders -- he'd rather throw bodies against the wall of your pass protection and find a weak point. Like water against a dam, it didn't really matter how many players the Packers kept in to protect -- if there was a weak point (which there often was), Flores had a rusher in that spot. His distinctive approach to early-down blitzing breaks the rules. It forces opposing offenses to play a different sport than the one for which they're prepared in the other 17 weeks of the season.

But Johnson knows Flores well. He called offense against him as the coordinator of the Lions -- twice in 2023, twice in 2024 -- then picked up another two games in 2025 as the head coach of the Bears. Across six matchups, Johnson's team is 5-1 -- the only loss was last season's opener and Williams' first start in Johnson's offense. Over those six games, Johnson's offense doesn't look like a 59-point monster ... but it's clearly better than the average offense against the marauding Vikings coordinator.

So what does Johnson do that other teams can't replicate? A few things stick out. The first is communication. Flores' defense requires as much pre-snap coordination between 11 defensive players as any defense in football -- that's why Harrison Smith is back and so valuable to this defense. He can be the coach on the field, changing the playcall after the defense sees the formation.

Johnson rises to meet Flores. His offense is as communication-heavy as any in the league, and his group is empowered to make adjustments based on what it sees. Flores wants to get opposing offenses stuck in a bad protection look or run call; Johnson's groups are elite at getting out of such sticky wickets. Williams' pre-snap command, which has reportedly taken big strides through Year 1 and into Year 2 with Johnson, will be tested here.

To challenge Flores' reliance on communication, Johnson will randomly snap the football quickly -- no motion, no checking. Immediate snaps. The Bears had 19 quick snaps against the Vikings in Week 11 -- snaps in which less than two seconds elapse between the line getting set and the ball being snapped. It was the most they had in any game last season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. Second most? The 17 such snaps in Week 1 ... also against Flores.

The second is formational. The Lions loved condensed sets under Johnson, and the Bears have continued that approach. Condensed sets are typically a bad idea against blitz-heavy teams. When you spread out the field, it's easier to identify suspicious defensive alignment that reveals who's blitzing from where. Against Flores and the Vikings, there's no point in trying to riddle things out -- the blitzes are too frequent and too varied. You'll think you're right, you'll actually be wrong, and then you'll be dead in the water.

So Johnson turns into the skid. He gets as condensed as possible against Flores. In 2025, no offense had more condensed formations in any game than the Bears in Week 11 against the Vikings, with an average formational width of only 17.7 yards. Teeny tiny formations allow Johnson to throw the ball on out-breakers into a ton of space, to stress the Vikings' cornerbacks who are typically insulated by trap coverages and quick throws. It also allows Johnson to meet Flores' duplicity and disguise with the beautiful simplicity of the running game. With lighter players such as Joshua Metellus and Dallas Turner on the edge against double-teams from extra tight ends and condensed wide receivers, the Bears can grind out physical yardage and set up the play-action pass.

Does Flores have an answer to this approach? Yes ... but not on the chalkboard. The Vikings' first three picks in the 2026 draft were trench picks: defensive tackle Caleb Banks in the first round, on/off-ball linebacker hybrid Jake Golday in the second round and another defensive tackle in the third round in space-gobbler Domonique Orange. Any defense that plays in a division with the Bears needs to be serious about its run defense -- doubly true for Flores, who will never get to third-and-long against Chicago unless he has some run-stuffing hog mollies up front to slow down Swift and Monangai.

Johnson won Assistant Coach of the Year in 2024. Second place in voting was Flores. When Flores was a young defensive assistant cutting his teeth in New England, Johnson was doing the same in Miami on offense -- twice a year, they saw each other. These two have circled their matchups like heavyweight fighters for years now, and on Sunday, we get another 90-minute dance in the ring. Bring your popcorn.

I think ... the Texans' offense will win some games this year
The Texans' defense was a machine last season, and it entered 2026 with all of the Super Bowl hype. Houston just needed an offense that could do enough to win those games in which the defense struggled.

Sunday was one such game. The Texans gave up 36 points to the Bills and lost. So did the offense fail to clear its low bar? Technically, yes. But I think the underlying signs were encouraging.

In the first game of Nick Caley's second season as the Texans' offensive coordinator, Houston was efficient. Explosiveness has never been an issue for C.J. Stroud-led offenses, but efficiency has been a problem. Against the Bills in a Week 1 loss, the Texans had an offensive success rate of 45.7% -- the ninth-best Stroud start. They had a first down conversion rate -- how many of their first-and-10s became a new first-and-10 or a touchdown -- of 78.1%, the sixth-best Stroud start.

Despite all of the offseason discussion around Stroud, the Texans' spike in Week 1 efficiency was not about the quarterback at all -- it was about the running game. With new running back David Montgomery and offseason additions Keylan Rutledge and Evan Brown along the offensive line, the Texans had a 60% success rate on runs between the tackles against the Bills, their second-best number in Stroud's career. On third/fourth down with 2 or fewer yards to go, the Texans had six runs and five conversions -- they hadn't had more than three in a game since 2023. Over the past three seasons combined, they were 25th in first down rate and 28th in stuff rate in the same context. They couldn't reliably get to a new set of downs. Now they can.

The presence of a functional running game is radically new. Houston ranked 31st in rushing success rate and EPA per rush over the past three seasons combined. It keeps Stroud from feeling as if he needs to make every play a haymaker, which draws out the worst of his play, as we saw last postseason. It also slows down the pass rush. Stroud was pressured on 21.4% of his dropbacks Sunday, per NFL Next Gen Stats.

The fourth-year quarterback still committed two brutal mistakes on pressured dropbacks -- a sack-fumble in his own territory that set up a Bills field goal and the sack-fumble to end the game. The Texans paid for right guard Ed Ingram largely because of his impact as a run blocker ... but he gave up the first-and-goal quick pressure to Deone Walker that set the Texans behind the sticks. With Braden Smith hurt, Trent Brown manned the right tackle spot -- another superior run blocker to pass protector. He gave up the quick pressure to Greg Rousseau that ended the game.

The Texans draw a Bengals team in Week 2 that, like the Bills, wants to play from two-high shells and drop into zone coverage. Buffalo forced two turnovers by Houston; Cincinnati took four from Tampa Bay in Week 1. If Houston continues to struggle with pass protection and ball security on key passing downs, the improvements in the running game won't mean much.

But for the bulk of that game, Stroud looked like his old self: calm, poised and aggressive. He drilled a beautiful touchdown to Nico Collins in the middle of the field in a play that was emblematic of much of his outing; Stroud threw 50.0% in-breaking routes against Buffalo, more than any other quarterback in Week 1. If Stroud can be the playmaker with his arm that he has been for much of his career in tandem with a more effective running game, the Texans should have the offense they've long needed to pair with their elite defense -- a balanced approach that gives them ability to hang in shootouts with the league's best offenses.

Buffalo was the first test of that. Cincinnati is another great offense with a gettable defense. Bengals QB Joe Burrow has a wicked quick time to throw -- over 70% of his passes were out in under 2.5 seconds against the Buccaneers. That quick game will neutralize the Texans' pass rush some, and Houston's offense will again be called upon to pick up some of the slack. It was nine yards away from answering the call in Week 1, and I find myself full of belief it will answer the call in Week 2 and the games to come.

I think ... four takeaways isn't the story of the Bengals' defense
Go out and buy yourself a defense. It's just that easy. Pay Bryan Cook and get a forced fumble on Bucky Irving. Pay Dexter Lawrence II, and he'll get the pressure that forces the checkdown to Irving that ends in the Cook fumble. Pay Boye Mafe and get another forced fumble on Baker Mayfield.

The Bengals forced and recovered four fumbles Sunday in a win over the Buccaneers. In the previous five seasons, there were only seven games of four-plus fumble recoveries. The Bengals also got high-value takeaways: One recovery was a scoop and score, another was in the end zone to prevent a Buccaneers touchdown, and two more were on the Buccaneers' side of the 50-yard line. The Bengals generated 18.6 expected points on fumbles in this game, the 16th-highest in a single game in the past 20 years.

It's easy to see a performance like that and scream "regression" from the mountaintops. And there will be regression because fumble luck is just that -- luck. But we can see the forest through the trees and take a look at how the Bengals' defense performed outside of the fumbles. And the outcome is interesting.

The Bengals put a blanket on top of the Buccaneers. Mayfield threw 50% of his passes behind the line of scrimmage -- a number that was well higher before garbage time. It's only the 13th game with at least half of the pass attempts behind the line over the past three seasons, and five of the 13 were backup quarterbacks. Cincinnati turned Mayfield -- typically one of our more downfield passers -- into a checkdown machine.

How? Team effort. The Bengals consistently found quick penetration from a variety of sources. Veteran defensive tackle Jonathan Allen got a red zone sack on a twist with Lawrence. Rookie second-round pass rusher Cashius Howell drew a flag on a play-action pass protection. Mafe flushed Mayfield into multiple quick scrambles. The Bengals' defensive backfield, as it did last season under defensive coordinator Al Golden, mixed man and zone coverage looks with a ton of middle-of-the-field help. It's hard to get a bead on what coverage the team is in on any given down.

Perhaps the Buccaneers wanted to test how well the Bengals would tackle, as Cincinnati was among the league's worst teams for missed tackle rate last season. There were a few odd early checkdowns from Mayfield -- like this second-and-10 in which he has Emeka Egbuka on the option route out of the backfield ... but passes on it to hasten to the RB checkdown. Whatever the agent behind this shallow approach, the Bengals tackled well all game.

If Cincinnati can be trusted to affect the pocket and tackle in space this season, then the defense is mightily improved. But that isn't enough. The Buccaneers still had a dropback success rate of 52.8% -- better than the Bengals' offense on the day. Mayfield completed 82.1% of his passes and had a 38.9% first down/touchdown rate, ninth among Week 1 passers. Only Lamar Jackson and the Ravens (173 yards) had more YAC than the Bucs (168).

When I first watched this film, I was impressed by how well the Bengals covered downfield (and still am). I think DJ Turner II and Dax Hill form one of the better young CB duos in the league. Upon second watch, I wonder if the Buccaneers played too far into the Bengals' hands and should have done more to test downfield windows. The young linebackers can still be moved in coverage, slot corner is a question, and safety Jordan Battle doesn't have great traits defending the pass in space.

Houston is next on the docket for Cincinnati, and as much as the Bengals won their game thanks to fumble recoveries, the Texans lost their game thanks in large part to two fumbles lost. The Texans are far from a perfect offense. Their reliance on Nico Collins at receiver should invite shadow coverage from Turner as Golden forces Stroud to beat him with other pass catchers. The theory in Cincinnati -- that the Bengals can force longer dropbacks and consistently pressure opposing quarterbacks -- should work against a Texans offensive line that's only average in pass protection. But without four fumbles, that formula might produce harsher results.

The Bengals' defensive overhaul is only in its infancy. The unit should deservedly play with confidence after Week 1 -- especially the new faces. What the defense is in Week 2 won't be what it is by Week 18. I'm excited to see it in a game without historic fumble production.

I think ... Dalton Kincaid is the Bills' secret sauce
The Bills made waves when they traded a second-round pick for Bears receiver DJ Moore. And Moore made waves in his first game with Josh Allen: 5 catches, 100 yards and a score -- not to mention a 46-yard pass interference penalty he drew that set the Bills up at the 1-yard line.

But Moore wasn't Buffalo's leading receiver in the win over the Texans. It was Kincaid with five receptions for 130 yards. It was the most receiving yards of his career and the most in a game for any Bills tight end since 1967.

It's easy to forget how high of hopes the Bills had for Kincaid when they drafted him with at No. 25 in 2023. We were in the throes of the flex tight end revolution thanks to a few historically productive years from the Chiefs' Travis Kelce, who finished the 2022 season third among all players in total receptions and eighth in total yards. Mark Andrews was the primary pass catcher for another AFC contender in Baltimore. The Bills wanted some of that.

Kincaid was not an immediate success, which glared relative to the rookie sensations of Kyle Pitts Sr. (2021) and Sam LaPorta (2023). We used to say tight ends took time to develop. But if rookies were hitting faster ... why did Kincaid have only 1,100 yards and four touchdowns across his first two seasons as a pro?

Whatever the reason, Kincaid's 2024 season was impeded by a PCL injury in Week 10. He played 66.6% of the team's snaps in the weeks before the injury and 43.2% in the games after he returned. That number was even lower (38.8%) in the 2025 season, when Kincaid was limited because that PCL continued to cause him issues. After a full offseason to recover, he entered the 2026 season unabated.

One week down, one week healthy. Kincaid played 72% of the offensive snaps in Week 1, his most in a game since Week 9 of 2024 -- the game before his PCL tear. The Bills had at least two tight ends on the field for 50% of their snaps, fourth among league offenses in Week 1.

Only these multi-TE sets ... are not multi-TE formations. Kincaid is truly a big receiver by both alignment and usage. He was in a tight end alignment on only three of his 22 routes (13.6%). Only the Panthers' Darren Waller and the Bengals' Mike Gesicki -- both of whom played half as many snaps -- were detached from the tackle more often in Week 1. No tight end took a greater number of snaps out wide than Kincaid's 15.

Take a look at this play. Kincaid starts out in a wide alignment, then motions into the formation as the ball is snapped. He gets a free release from the stack and hits the line of scrimmage with momentum. He clears safety Reed Blankenship, who's playing to Kincaid's low hip and is worried about a crossing route. But Kincaid, who can eat up ground and change direction like a wideout, bends this route back to the corner while outdistancing Blankenship -- resulting in an easy pitch and catch downfield.

The reason Blankenship is so worried about the crosser is because Kincaid can run them -- and run away from corners when he does so. Here, Kincaid is in a snug alignment in 13 personnel. Out of the two-minute warning and still trailing, the Bills go for a two-man route combo off play-action -- all their chips in on Moore on a clear out and Kincaid on a crosser. Kincaid beats Kamari Lassiter to the spot, survives contact and makes another defender miss. Thanks in large part to this play, Kincaid ended the day with 42 total yards after the catch and 20 YAC over expectation, by NFL Next Gen Stats' model -- the most YAC over expectation of a single game in his career.

The only reason the Bills' recent 12 and 13 personnel obsession works is because Kincaid has legitimate receiver skills. It isn't just the ability to run past a defensive back or break a tackle. Kincaid tracks the football down the field better than almost any other tight end. Since the start of last season, he has averaged 9.8 air yards per target, second to Gesicki. He has a 14.4% first down rate on routes and a 10.3% explosive reception rate on routes. Those rate stats benefit some from Kincaid's limited snap count in 2025, but the point still stands. He does the thing that players at the tight end position aren't supposed to be able to do: create big plays.

Watch this catch over Derek Stingley Jr., an All-Pro corner. Watch Kincaid jockey for positioning as the ball enters its arc, figure out where it's landing with plenty of time to reposition, then elevate and win the ball in the air. This is Tee Higgins-esque behavior. Tight ends don't do this.

In that Moore is the shiny new receiver in Buffalo, it is easy to attribute any and all offensive improvement from the Bills this season to his appearance. But I would argue it is the skill set of Kincaid -- who can 1) keep the Bills in multi-TE sets and 2) make WR-esque plays down the field -- that clarifies Moore's role. The Bills were in 13 personnel on 20 snaps against the Texans on Sunday. On eight of those snaps, Moore was the lone receiver. Running 13 personnel forces opponents into base defense and single-high coverages. It makes them predictable and easier to pass against, and Moore feasts at that table -- but only because Kincaid laid it out for him.

This particular stressor is interesting as we enter Week 2, in which the Bills play the Lions on "Thursday Night Football." Over the past few seasons, no defense in the league more willingly plays base defense than Detroit (though the Lions were in base only 26% of the time in Week 1, a new wrinkle from defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard). The Bills will still invite that base defense by lining up in multi-TE sets. And this time, when Kincaid is the widest receiver in the formation, he won't have to contend with Stingley or Lassiter ... he'll get Rock Ya-Sin and D.J. Reed instead. The Lions' defense just gave up 410 passing yards to Tyler Shough and the Saints. What do you think they'll do to Josh Allen?

Four years after the Bills picked Kincaid, we might finally get a view of what they envisioned for him. And if he continues producing explosive receptions at a 70% snap rate, he -- along with Moore -- will reintroduce the verticality the offense has lacked these past few years. If there's another level to find in the Joe Brady-Josh Allen pairing in Buffalo, it's through Kincaid.

I think ... the Titans score 0 points in Week 2
I cannot remember a team that looked less functional on offense in Week 1 than the Titans in Sunday's loss to the Jets. I went back and looked at the past few seasons of Week 1 travesties -- Russell Wilson's Giants had six points in 2025; Daniel Jones' Giants had six points in 2024; Jones' Giants also had zero points in 2023; oh my goodness, are all of these just Giants games? -- and I still don't remember seeing something I found this particularly problematic.

The Titans looked as if they had never played together before. Second-year quarterback Cam Ward was consistently out of time with his receivers, and his trademark laissez-faire approach in the pocket spelled disaster as he tried to hit open receivers in time. Both tackles were brutal in pass protection, while fifth-round rookie Fernando Carmona predictably struggled in his first career start at right guard.

Offensive tackle JC Latham, one of the league's most penalized players in 2025, started off 2026 with two more flags. Running back Tyjae Spears dropped a 2-yard pass that hit him so squarely it almost bisected him. Rookie receiver Carnell Tate didn't make an effort to catch a third-down crossing route that looked somewhat catchable. Second-year receiver Elic Ayomanor turned Ward's best throw of the day into an incompletion by jumping for a ball he didn't need to and getting shoved out of bounds for his elevation.

What was coordinator Brian Daboll up to? I simply cannot tell. Ward had three dropbacks with three or fewer routes in the concept -- that's a play with at least seven players in pass protection -- and yet Ward was pressured on all three dropbacks.

There was a fake reverse shot play that I just have to show you. The run-action is meant to manipulate the linebackers and defensive backs to the wide side of the field ... but the routes break to the other side of the field. What's the point of the fake if it doesn't move anyone you need moved?

I thought Daboll would be good for Ward because he would encourage him to scramble more, and he did -- Ward had four scrambles, tying his season high from his rookie year. But I also thought Daboll would open up easy-access completions in the RPO game. Ward missed the first RPO offered to him -- a swing route to Wan'Dale Robinson -- so badly it skipped off the turf and the Titans largely passed on RPOs after that.

After watching the way the Titans' offensive line struggled against the Jets (they made Kingsley Enagbare look like Maxx Crosby), I cannot bear the idea of the Titans' upcoming game against Philadelphia. The Eagles' front was as dominant as ever against a poor Commanders line in Week 1. It collected 19 pressures, a single-game best in the Vic Fangio era, despite the fact that starting edge rusher Jonathan Greenard wasn't even healthy enough to play.

I have no idea what to hang my hat on with this Week 1 Titans performance. They blew assignments and blocks in the running game. They went no-huddle but couldn't disrupt the defense with pace. They found no YAC and couldn't get the ball to anyone in space. There's nothing here.

The Titans are 7-point underdogs to the Eagles with a projected total of 39.5 points, according to DraftKings. That means the sportsbook is projecting the Titans to score around 15.5 points. Under, under, under.

I think ... the Lions' secondary is going to be an Achilles' heel
The Lions face the Bills on "Thursday Night Football" this week. Two teams that won in the final seconds of Week 1. Two teams that have made postseason runs recently but have not played on a Super Bowl Sunday -- and are desperate to do so. Gimme, gimme, gimme.

I have my suspicions about both defenses after one week of NFL action. The Bills blew a few coverages and run fits in their first game under coordinator Jim Leonhard, and their lack of size in the back seven is notable. But their warts pale in comparison to the nasty boil that is the Lions' secondary.

Detroit got the drop on the Saints with a nickel-heavy, zone-heavy approach -- a zag from its defensive identity. In the first half (i.e. before the game script was clear pass for the Saints), the Lions were in zone coverage on 87.5% of the Saints' dropbacks, higher than any game last season under Kelvin Sheppard save for a Week 18 contest in which they were already mathematically eliminated from playoff contention. Of their 34 defensive plays, 20 were in nickel personnel -- their second highest of any game under Sheppard.

This zone-heavy approach worked well to protect the Lions' older corners, D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin, from chasing receivers all across the formation. In the absence of Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch (both on the physically unable to perform list), the Lions had Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox and Thomas Harper playing the safety and nickel roles -- not the sort of talent you want isolated in man coverage against slots and tight ends, either.

Then the Saints circled the wagons in the locker room and adjusted. Quarterback Tyler Shough had a towering 325 passing yards in the second half and overtime combined. Since the 2010 season, only 11 quarterbacks have been so prolific after the halftime break.

Shough's first big completion out of the halftime locker room (after a pick and two sacks to open the third quarter) was a scramble drill play. The Lions were well positioned, but once Chris Olave broke downfield, it became a footrace between him and Reed -- a losing proposition for Detroit.

Detroit's corners were playing with a ton of cushion -- in part to trap underneath throws with driving defensive backs and sinking linebackers, but also to give their corners room to deal with the speed of Olave and rookie receiver Bryce Lance, a 4.3 player. Reed averaged 7.1 yards of pre-snap cushion, per NFL Next Gen Stats; Ya-Sin was just behind him at 5.9 yards. Last season, Ya-Sin was the second-closest CB to the line of scrimmage (4.0 yards of cushion), and Reed was well closer than average (5.2 yards).

No matter what sort of scheme you run or cushion you deploy, speed liabilities at cornerback will come back to get you. The Bills don't have a particularly fast group of receivers, but it's this sort of out-of-structure play that Josh Allen will create far more often -- and far more successfully -- than Shough did.

So, this is a shift, and it's to insulate the safety play. I'm not sure how tenable it is. The Saints' ability to get free access on slants in the second half was a big part of their comeback. Olave and Lance both got open on deep stop routes, as well, as the Lions' secondary kept a careful umbrella over any vertical routes. Against a quarterback with Allen's velocity on Thursday, those windows will be wide open. Of course, against a quarterback with Allen's aggressiveness, Sheppard's clever zone coverage calls also could generate big negative plays. But the Lions had two picks, a sack-fumble recovered and four more sacks against the Saints -- and still, New Orleans was a two-point try away from an upset.

The Lions are 1-0 after one week without Branch and Joseph -- that's a huge win. I'm just mightily worried about their ability to stay afloat against a more developed quarterback and deeper passing attack.

I think ... Trevor Lawrence is the league MVP
Do I really have an opinion about the league MVP through one week of the season? Absolutely not. But the mind wanders into such fantasies when the Jaguars' offense cruise controls its way to a 34-point outing against a not-insignificant Browns defense in Week 1.

Lawrence's lightbulb flicked on midway through his first year in coach Liam Coen's offense. The trade acquisition of Jakobi Meyers and midseason breakout of Parker Washington sure helped. With a new cadre of wide receivers, the Jaguars pushed the ball downfield at league-leading rates after their Week 8 bye. Lawrence was fourth in the league in air yards per attempt (9.7) and third in the percentage of his pass attempts that were at least 10 yards downfield (41.2%).

Against the Browns in Week 1, he picked up exactly where he left off with 11.2 air yards per attempt, 47.8% of his throws going at least 10 yards downfield and a whopping 56.5% of his throws beyond the sticks.

Lawrence can have disastrous outcomes when he's just blindly throwing first reads into tight coverage -- we saw plenty of those games in the past five years -- but with a great schemer in Coen and a talented pass catching group, he's a total flamethrower. And as Lawrence plays with more confidence in structure, he makes better plays outside of structure, where his escapability and throw-on-the-move talent has always been underappreciated and underused. His best play of the day was his fourth touchdown -- a second-and-19 scramble drill in which he shows off just how well he can drive the football when moving to his left.

I don't think the Browns' defense is a pushover in 2026 without Myles Garrett -- Denzel Ward, Jared Verse, Carson Schwesinger and Grant Delpit are all still pretty good players. But maybe it is, and every quarterback will walk all over it. Here are the Jaguars' next five opponents: Broncos, Patriots, Bengals, Eagles and Texans. Three of the league's four best defenses from last season ... and the Bengals and Patriots are far from easy. If the Jaguars and Lawrence are for real, we're only a few games from knowing so for sure.

Five things I might think

I might think ... that the Bears should trade for Joey Porter Jr. The Steelers' corner sat out Week 1 as he and the team continue to stare each other down amid contract extension talks. If the Steelers really do want to trade him -- and my sense so far is that they don't -- I think the Bears are the right team to make the call. Chicago has the future cap space necessary to give Porter a big long-term deal and should do anything and everything it can to build a halfway-decent defense around this stupendous offense.

I might think ... that the 13 personnel hype met expectations. In all the excitement around new coaches and final results, nobody has really checked on our favorite offseason schematic trend: 13 personnel, or three-TE sets. There were 160 total snaps of 13 personnel across the league this week, the most such snaps since the start of the 2007 season (as far back as my database goes). For some teams (like the Bills above) it makes so much. For others, it doesn't really. I think we see this number fall back down to earth by midseason.

I might think ... the Ravens' offense already peaked. The Colts' defense was high on my list for Potentially Awful Groups in 2026 -- and boy was it Sunday. We haven't seen enough football yet to accurately apportion credit to the Ravens' offense and blame to the Colts' defense for the Ravens' 41 points. Baltimore might not see such smooth sailing for the rest of the season -- doubly so if Zay Flowers' hamstring continues to flare up regularly. The Ravens were thin at receiver before they lost rookie Ja'Kobi Lane to injured reserve because of a fractured wrist.

I might think ... the same about the Giants' offense. Speaking of defenses worthy of suspicion, the Cowboys' coverage woes carried over from 2025 to 2026 in their "Sunday Night Football" loss to the Giants. Brian Schottenheimer openly lamented multiple coverage busts by "young players" in his postgame news conference. New York was able to burn clock and limit the second half to only five total possessions -- tied for the least second-half drives in a game over the past 15 seasons. I thought Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart looked quite sharp and the offensive line looked ferocious, but I'd like to see them in a game in which the opposing defense has a bit more spine.

I might think ... the Cardinals are going to be good(ish). The story coming out of the Cardinals' upset win over the Chargers as 9-point favorites is all about Justin Herbert's bad performance and the failed promise of the Mike McDaniel offense. I'm far more interested in Jacoby Brissett ripping in-breakers to Kendrick Bourne, Michael Wilson and Trey McBride. Arizona and new head coach Mike LaFleur were hitting the McVay classics flawlessly in Week 1. The Cardinals have a solid line that should produce a more exciting running game as rookie Jeremiyah Love's ankle sprain heals. Long term, the quarterback position will be a limiting factor. But the Cardinals are not a Dolphins/Browns tier team -- not even close.

stories.headline: All 20 Premier League teams ranked: Which managers will be fired first?
stories.summary: The Premier League is a constant carousel of coaches being fired and hired. Who's safe and who's on the chopping block? Let's rank everyone!
stories.body:
While we've been heading in this direction for a while, we truly entered a new era of Premier League managing this past summer.

With the professionalization and corporatization of Premier League front offices, the all-powerful manager who picks the squad, scouts transfers, cuts the grass, and selects the color of the table linens in the canteen has nearly become extinct. Whether this is a good thing is up for debate. Whether this is actually happening is not.

Of the league's 20 managers, only one of them has been with his current club for four years. Only nine have been in their current position for a year or more. And half of the current coaches haven't even had the gig for 200 days. Michael Carrick was named Manchester United's full-time manager in late May, and he's more tenured than half of the other coaches in the Premier League.

As clubs have moved away from the manager-decides-all model, they haven't just stripped away responsibilities from the man on the sideline. No, they've seemingly decided that the person in that position is disposable, too. Ten different managers were fired during last season, and then six more left their positions after the season ended.

What this all means, among many other things: it's never too early to check in on the Hot Seat Index. We've only played four games, but as the numbers suggest, someone is going to get fired soon, and then a bunch of other guys are going to lose their jobs soon after that.

This is not a celebration of rising unemployment rates -- rather, it's a check-in on the state of play across all 20 Premier League clubs. Who is the safest on the sideline? And who might be gone with one more stale result? We've ranked all 20 manager jobs in the league, from least likely to be fired to the most likely.

The last of his kind

20. Mikel Arteta, Arsenal

It's not an exaggeration to say that we're never going to see another Premier League manager like Mikel Arteta. Arsenal showed extreme patience over his first few seasons with the club, including after eighth-place and fifth-place league finishes -- and now they've got a Premier League title, look to be sizable favorites to grab another, and are simply just one of the best teams in the world.

At six-plus years with Arsenal, Arteta is -- by far -- the longest-tenured manager in the league, and he's the only coach in the league to win the Premier League. But he's also the second-youngest manager to ever win the Premier League after Jose Mourinho's first two titles with Chelsea.

It's not just the longevity, though. As more and more clubs are making a point of hiring "head coaches" rather than "managers," Arteta was eventually promoted from head coach to manager.

He's the most powerful coach in the league, as it seems pretty clear that he's the one driving the club's recruitment over the past two seasons. After years of building up the roster by signing early- and pre-prime talent, they've shifted toward acquiring the kind of win-now players (mid-to-late 20s) that managers tend to favor.

Given how almost every club functions at this point, it's really hard to see any other coach ever again reaching Arteta's current perch: controlling most of the major decisions at one of the richest clubs in the world.

Managers at clubs where managers don't matter

19. Keith Andrews, Brentford

The impact of coaches on performance across all professional sports is both hard to measure and almost definitely overstated. Brentford and Brighton are aware of this, but despite that organizational knowledge, they don't take it to mean that you should hire and fire coaches for fun.

18. Fabian Hurzeler, Brighton

Instead, the clubs like Brentford and Brighton value their coaches as, well, coaches. They have structured recruiting systems and preferred styles of play, and then they have a list of guys who they think will fit into it.

This doesn't lead to job insecurity for their coaches. Rather, it means that they already have a sense of who they might hire if the current coach decides to leave or gets scooped up by a bigger club.

It's way too early

17. Enzo Maresca, Manchester City

Despite playing their toughest game of the season with only 10 players for 70-plus minutes, Man City have been every bit as good as Arsenal through the first four matches.

They're going to challenge for the Premier League title, and they're going to challenge for the Champions League title. Barring some unforeseen downturn not driving by injury, Maresca isn't going anywhere anytime soon.

16. Andoni Iraola, Liverpool

Liverpool are one of the most patient clubs in the league -- or, at least, they were. Then they fired Arne Slot just a year after he won the club's second-ever Premier League title, and now they have a new, sizable minority-ownership group.

But for all the question marks over this summer's transfer strategy, it certainly seems like the club is aware that they're in the middle of a rebuild. They're definitely not trying to maximize performance for this season, at least. While it's been quite a "meh" first four matches, things would have to go really poorly for Iraola's job to be at risk.

They wouldn't ... right?

15. Unai Emery, Aston Villa

Ironically, the two longest tenured Premier League managers are Mikel Arteta and the guy Mikel Arteta replaced at Arsenal. The reason Emery isn't earlier on this list -- despite his team overachieving their resources and talent year after year -- is that there's at least the chance the bottom falls out. Villa have replaced basically every key player from the best Villa side of the Premier League era -- and they've done it all in one summer.

Through four games, they've been arguably the worst team in the league. By adjusted goal differential (70% non-penalty xG difference, 30% goal difference), they rank dead last:

At the same time, they started last season in the exact same way -- and then finished fourth.

Totally fine -- for now

14. David Moyes, Everton

This club was battling relegation not too long ago, and now they're as close to league-average as it gets. Expected goals, shots, penalty area touches -- they're creating almost exactly as many as they're conceding through four matches.

13. Daniel Farke, Leeds United

Only Emery and Arteta have been in their jobs longer than Farke, who's been at Leeds for three years and change. And for the second season running, Leeds look competent. They're fifth on the adjusted goal differential chart, and after finishing roughly even last season.

Longer term, there's the question of if this ownership group, with the built-in commercial power at the club, is happy with competence, but that's a question for the offseason.

12. Regis Le Bris, Sunderland

The schedule hasn't been particularly hard, but after surviving -- and frankly, thriving -- last season thanks to an unsustainable run of hot finishing, they've outshot their opponents across the first four matches and played Arsenal way more tightly than anyone else has so far this season.

Le Bris is the fourth-longest-tenured manager in the league, and his team looks safer than they did at the start of the season.

11. Marco Rose, AFC Bournemouth

We're splitting the difference here. Rose's high-wire style has the potential to completely fall apart, and three points from four matches is relegation-level form. But they've outshot their opponents, and their adjusted goal differential is right around league average.

If they're able to stick to this process, things should turn around, but that's one of the tricks of managerial success: knowing what you're doing is working despite poor results, and then convincing your players, and your bosses, that it's true.

10. Matthias Jassle, Newcastle United

Newcastle under Jassle are sometimes maybe good, sometimes maybe lose to Leeds 4-1.

They've come back to earth after four points from the opening pair of matches against Liverpool and Spurs, and they're fortunate to be where they currently are in the table. But the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, maybe the richest ownership group in all of sports, doesn't seem to feel much urgency around Newcastle -- they've said goodbye to all of their best players and replaced them with a bunch of year-away-from-being-a-year-away prospects. As long as they don't drift into the relegation battle, Jassle should be safe.

Can a promoted manager ever be safe?

9. Sergej Jakirovic, Hull City

They're still one of the favorites to be relegated -- with greater-than-50% odds of going down wherever you look. But also: they've already played Manchester United and Chelsea ... and they're currently in third place. As in, behind only Manchester City and Arsenal.

And sure, the eight points from four games is fluky -- a plus-3 non-penalty goal differential from a minus-3 xG differential -- but this was supposed to be one of the worst teams in Premier League history. So far, they're not even close to the worst team in the Premier League this season.

8. Gary O'Neil, Ipswich Town

Ipswich's outlook is even better -- their relegation odds have already dipped below 50% after wins in two of their first four matches. But this is about as high as you could reasonably put Jakirovic and O'Neil. Both teams are still very likely to end up in a relegation battle, and when that's the case, your seat never really cools down.

Can the manager of these clubs ever be safe?

7. Xabi Alonso, Chelsea

Sure, he's signed through 2030, and yeah: Chelsea are currently in fourth place. But this team still hasn't played a convincing 90 minutes of soccer. After a wild first three matches where Chelsea barely had any possession but scored lots of goals, last weekend's home game against Hull was an opportunity for Chelsea to show that they could dominate a game against a theoretically bad team.

Instead, uh ...

Purple are shots, orange are goals, and the larger the circle, the higher the xG.

They don't have a midweek Champions League game to point to as an excuse, either. Under current ownership, I'm not sure any Chelsea manager could be higher than, say, 10 on this list. And Alonso's team needs to stabilize before he moves up any higher.

6. Michael Carrick, Manchester United

Man United are unlucky to only have four points from their first four matches. They've turned a plus-2.5 non-penalty xG difference into a minus-1 goal difference. And they've attempted 83 shots and conceded just 41.

At the same time, they've faced one of the easiest schedules in the league: Hull, Ipswich, Everton, and then 70-plus minutes with an extra man against Manchester City.

United only signed Carrick to a two-year contract -- essentially the minimum level of commitment you can show to a non-interim manager. And with the added burden of Champions League matches this season, things aren't going to get any easier from here on out.

5. Oliver Glasner, Nottingham Forest

Forest have been quite good so far. They've edged their opponents on xG, shots, and penalty touches. They're already, pretty clearly, an Oliver Glasner team: low possession, but aggressive without the ball and frightening whenever they win it back. At most clubs, he'd be somewhere in the top 10, or even top five of this list.

Unfortunately, Forest have the most volatile, unpredictable owner in ... all of professional sports? A couple unfortunate results, and Glasner could be out of a job before Christmas.

The hottest of hot seats

4. Alvaro Arbeloa, Fulham

They have one point, and his Fulham players are already staging protests on Instagram. This comes just months after his players were brawling in the training room at Real Madrid. We continue to have zero evidence that Arbeloa is a good manager, and we continue to have zero evidence that he's able to control a locker room.

But he was also allowed to sign a bunch of his former Real Madrid players, so Fulham seem somewhat committed. And two of his first four matches were against Chelsea and Liverpool.

3. Pierre Sage, Crystal Palace

By any metric, this is the worst defensive team in the league. They're last in goals conceded, xG allowed, shots conceded, and penalty-area touches allowed.

A lot of that has to do with the fact that three-fifths of their defense from the Glasner Era are no longer with the club. But the balance is off -- can Sage, who had a fantastic season with Lens last year, figure out a way to fix it?

2. Roberto De Zerbi, Tottenham Hotspur

After spending $400 million dollars to avoid another relegation scare, Tottenham ... are right back where they were last season. They've yet to win a match, yet to score a single goal, and have the fourth-worst adjusted goal differential in the league through four matches.

For all of his talents in building unique possession systems, De Zerbi has never shown the ability to manage his way out of adversity. The press conferences are already getting testy, and although he's signed through 2030, this one feels like it's a few more bad results from getting really bad.

1. Frank Lampard, Coventry City

Zero goals? Zero points? Yep, that'll do it.

stories.headline: NHL superstar poll: Rule changes, Texas expansion, fan culture
stories.summary: We asked a panel of stars at the NHL/NHLPA player media tour for their takes on a variety of hot topics.
stories.body:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- With training camps opening up this week, I caught up with over two dozen NHL superstars to get their takes on vital and trivial issues.

Some of hockey's biggest names discuss NHL rule changes they'd like to see; how an 84-game regular season will impact them; how they feel about the current state of fan culture; as well as their offseason life highlights and what they'd name a new expansion team in Houston or Austin, Texas.

Interviews were conducted at the NHL/NHLPA player media tour last week in Las Vegas. Enjoy!

How to watch the 2026-27 NHL season on ESPN networks, including 100 exclusive games and the out-of-market package (over 1,050 games).

What was your favorite experience of the summer?
"My dad finding out he got into the Hall of Fame. He honestly played it off so cool. But that first moment of him telling us, you could see the smile on his face. That was pretty special." -- Brady Tkachuk, Florida Panthers

"Lots of concerts. I went to Luke Combs, which was actually an awesome concert. Got to meet him afterward, and he was just an amazing guy. I mean, he's a Hurricanes fan, so I wasn't happy about that, but he was an amazing guy." -- Matthew Schaefer, New York Islanders

"We did a family trip to Cabo. It's nice to get away from real life for a minute and just shut everything down and just be present with your family. My wife and three kids, and then my parents and my aunt and uncle. The more, the merrier." -- Tage Thompson, Buffalo Sabres

"Going to the World Cup final. Got to go with a bunch of buddies, so it made it fun." -- Trevor Zegras, Philadelphia Flyers

"I just went to Spain with my family. Mallorca. Just chilled there and didn't do much." -- Leo Carlsson, Anaheim Ducks

"Our family did a little get-together in Michigan, just on the lake, on the water. We all took five days off and just spent time together, fished, hung out, played games. Caught a couple bass, pike. It was really good fishing waters. I had my girlfriend out, and she was out-fishing me, catching these huge bass. It was pretty sad." -- Frank Nazar, Chicago Blackhawks

"My favorite experience was flying back home to Stockholm for a week and bringing my two older kids. They're now 6 and 5 years old and they really hadn't experienced Sweden because they were 1 and 2 last time they went. It was just so awesome getting to see my hometown through their eyes for the first time. Showing them where I grew up and seeing all of our Swedish friends and family. So it was really great. That was my absolute favorite week of the summer." -- Gabriel Landeskog, Colorado Avalanche

"I got married in Vancouver just with our families, and then we had a big celebration in Minnesota. I actually was a little nervous. I didn't think I was going to get nervous, but yeah, I was a little nervous for the whole wedding part." -- Brock Boeser, Vancouver Canucks

"My day with the Cup. It was a good day with friends, family, and then got to eat some really good food out of it. Some barbecue and a Slavin Sundae: ice cream, brownies, Heath bits, chocolate fudge, red sprinkles." -- Jaccob Slavin, Carolina Hurricanes

"I went to Scotland on a golf trip. That was probably my favorite. A couple good rounds, actually. Overall, it was just cool to experience those courses." -- Alex DeBrincat, Detroit Red Wings

"I was able to buy a cottage up in Muskoka [Ontario], so just being able to share that with my family. I had some friends up there. It was pretty cool." -- Quinton Byfield, Los Angeles Kings

"My newborn. That's the best experience I could have asked for." -- Zach Werenski, Columbus Blue Jackets

"I had a kid. It's been awesome." -- Jack Eichel, Vegas Golden Knights

The NHL is adding another team in Texas, in either Houston or Austin. What would you like for them to be called?
"The Houston Humidity." -- Wyatt Johnston, Dallas Stars

"I guess it depends what city. But maybe the Rattlers or something?" -- Thompson

"It's got to be something bull-riding related maybe. Rodeo-related. Bull Riders. There you go." -- Jack Hughes, New Jersey Devils

"The Houston Hammers." -- Jamie Drysdale, Flyers

"The Austin Cattle." -- Eichel

"The Ranchers." -- Boeser

"The Mustangs." -- Macklin Celebrini, San Jose Sharks

"The Houston Aeros. Run it back." -- Cole Caufield, Montreal Canadiens

"The Butt-Kickers. Because of the boots." -- Filip Forsberg, Nashville Predators

"I was going to say Cowboys. I think it's baller. Would make a sick logo, too." -- Logan Cooley, Utah Mammoth

"Maybe the Houston Sparks? Spurs, Sparks? I don't know." -- Slavin

"The Wranglers. Oh no, that's Calgary. Eh, we can do the same name for Texas." -- Tkachuk

"Every time I think of Texas, I just keep thinking of other teams' names. I mean, I like the Longhorns." -- Byfield

"Texas Hockey Club." -- Zegras

"Not for me to decide." -- Tom Wilson, Washington Capitals

How will your life be impacted by an 84-game season?
"My life will not be impacted by it." -- Matt Coronato, Calgary Flames

"I don't think it will be. Now, we play four preseason games, and I can only play two. And previously we had seven, so at the end of the day, I think you're still really playing the same amount of games." -- Thompson

"Impacted for the better. Shorter training camp, less preseason games. I feel like it just kind of becomes a drag a little bit when you're playing four preseason games." -- Werenski

"Just more time on the ice. Nothing better than that." -- Tkachuk

"I feel like the beginning of the season is going to be a little more offensively open. Obviously, having a bunch of preseason games and longer training camp gets you into your structure a little bit more and a little more comfortable. So, I feel like the start might be a little more chaotic, but it's just two more games, and I'm excited to play more hockey." -- Byfield

"I think the fact that they started the season early to spread out the games, I think we won't notice it as much." -- Jake Guentzel, Tampa Bay Lightning

"I think once you get past the 50-game mark, it kind of blends, to be honest with you. So, I think the extra two and probably the two preseason games that you miss out on will kind of even out." -- Drysdale

"Shorter preseason is going to be huge. But more back-to-back [games], which is going to be a shame." -- Zegras

"I don't think it really changes much. I think once you're in the grind and you just keep focused on that and a couple extra games won't be a big deal." -- Wilson

"I don't think it'll be too bad. Two extra games. Eighty-two is a lot of games; 84, you're not feeling any necessarily different, I think. I think we'll all be alright." -- Matty Beniers, Seattle Kraken

"I think your total workload for the year with the shortened preseason is pretty similar. Maybe you get a chance to get a couple more points." -- Robert Thomas, St. Louis Blues

"I'm excited. Two more games is always fun when you can play more hockey." -- Schaefer

"More chances to shoot the puck." -- Caufield

If you could change or drop one rule in the NHL, what would it be?
"Not so much of a rule as it's a judgment call, but it's when you call a tripping and an embellishment at the same time. Oh my God, it drives me nuts. And I'm always talking to the refs about it, and they're like, 'Well, I don't know.' It's really like it just has to be one or the other. I think that's common sense. I understand there can be a little bit of both, but if you're giving out a penalty, just pick one. Which one was worse? Was the dive worse or was the tripping worse?" -- Landeskog

"If you score on a power play, they don't come out of the box. You just keep your power play. Full two minutes, no matter what." -- Coronato

"Icing the puck on the penalty kill. Hate it." -- Zegras

"I just think if you score a short-hand goal, the guy's penalty should be done." -- Guentzel

"Delay of game. Puck over the glass. I don't think there's a person in the history of the game who purposefully puts the puck over the glass." -- Drysdale

"The puck-over-the-glass penalty. I've had too many of those. I won the Lady Byng [in 2020-21], and my one penalty was puck over the glass. That's not why I'm against it, but that's just a good example of it being a silly penalty." -- Slavin

"The league's always looking for more goals. Fans want more goals. If you took away goals being taken down because of a kicking motion, I think that's something that would instantly change it. You'd have a lot more goals. I think, also, if you're skilled enough to be able to use your feet to redirect the puck or kick it when you're tied up in front of the net, I think that should be a goal. I mean, obviously, you don't want guys just kicking at it all the time. I get the injury-prevention stuff there. But, at the same time, it's not as much of a true kicking where your blade's coming up. If you've worked hard enough and you put the puck in the net, it should be a goal." -- Thompson

"Getting kicked out of the faceoff. I might be be the guy who got kicked out the most." -- Byfield

"How the rookies have to wear helmets during warmups. I'd love to take a bucket off. I think that'd be nice." -- Schaefer

"No offsides. Get a few more breakaways." -- Cooley

"Just take off offsides completely. Play it like it's roller hockey where you could just be anywhere on the ice. The whole game would change. Like, do you take the power play and let the guy just cherry pick all the way down? But then he might have a breakaway. And I think the whole game would be different." -- Nazar

"The rule where when we dump it in on the goalie, sometimes we're not allowed to change. I don't know what the point of that rule." -- Boeser

"I honestly would let people travel day of games if they want to. Sometimes, we do it for Christmas games, usually where we go to St. Louis. But instead of flying the day before, for us, to Carolina or Detroit, some of those cities where you can just morning skate at home and go right to the game type of thing." -- Forsberg

"I like goalies playing the puck, so I would take out the dead space in the corners. The trapezoid. Especially with our goalies." -- Thomas

"Goals on high sticks, like tip-ins. I say if it looks like a skill, I think it should be counted." -- Caufield

"Add more time to 3-on-3 overtime. I don't love the shootout. I would rather someone wins in overtime. So, instead of five [minutes], maybe 15 or 10 or even 20. I don't know." -- Beniers

"I think the league's really good now. Anything that continues to keep guys healthy and safe and limit big injuries, I'm a proponent of, but I think the league's in a good spot." -- Quinn Hughes, Minnesota Wild

"The one thing is the offsides [review]. It's so hard, but at some point, it's like if you're a centimeter off 30 seconds before the goal, I think just leave it as a good goal. I think it's better for the game. I think that's where it gets hard though, because it's like in a playoff game you might be upset that it was offside, but I don't know what the right way to do it is. You think with AI now, you could almost just have it automatic, like they have in soccer for the offside." -- Johnston

"The offside review, when it's long after the play. If it's offside and they score right away, it should be offside. But if it's 30 seconds after and then the team scores, it's like, 'Oh, come on.' It doesn't affect the play. But I do love it when the other team scores, and then it's offside." -- Carlsson

"I think we're getting pretty nitpicky on all these different rules, like leg up over the blue line, all the cameras. Too much gets screwed up. As we get crazier and crazier, it's just counterproductive. I just want to go back and play it like it was in the 1800s or whenever the game was invented." -- Wilson

How do you feel about hockey fan culture in 2026, like how they engage with you in person and on social media?
"They're passionate, that's for sure. So, you've got to love the passion." -- Tkachuk

"I think it's great, with the way the game's trending and the amount of attention it's getting. Social media obviously has kind of been pushing that. Fans being able to interact with players a little bit more than they've been used to is something that they like. I know from a few of my buddies, they love following along with a lot of the behind-the-scenes stuff and things that fans usually don't get to see -- the curtain being pulled back for some of these fans that have been watching hockey for a long time." -- Thompson

"I love our fans in the league. They make it special. The playoffs in Minnesota are amazing. Dallas was great. Colorado was great. I try not to focus too much on engagement and social media and whatnot, just because there's a lot of negativity out there. But when you run into a fan in person and they're just a true fan of the game; that's always nice to see." -- Quinn Hughes

"I think obviously everything online is crazy, but I think 2026 was a great year for hockey and its fans, just with Olympics and the brand and the young talent coming up. I think there's a lot of players that people can root for." -- Jack Hughes

"I love it. There are definitely a lot more rivalries online. You can feel it in arenas and it's fun. I think we're starting to get more and more European soccer atmospheres at games, and it's starting to grow in that area. I think the more involved fans are in the game, the more you feel them on the ice; it's just awesome." -- Thomas

"I love it. When I'm in Chicago, I get a lot of great, positive things. I'm walking down the street, someone will be like, 'Hey man, let's go this year. Good luck.' I love that stuff. I think it's great. The fans are what make the sport, right? Yeah. I mean, we're here to play hockey and entertain, but they're what keeps the stadium full and what keeps us wanting to go back at it day in, day out." -- Nazar

"I think there's a great momentum behind the game right now. Obviously, everybody has an avenue to say whatever they want at any time, so that's always interesting. But it's part of the gig." -- Wilson
